pages.title: The NPPE at a glance

blocks.text: This guide prepares you for the National Professional Practice Examination (NPPE), the law and ethics exam most Canadian engineering and geoscience regulators require before granting a P.Eng. or P.Geo. licence. It follows the six content areas of the NPPE blueprint, in the same order, so every page you read maps to marks on the exam.
Each section has the same parts:

items.text: **What the exam tests**: the blueprint topics for that area and roughly how many questions they carry.
**Core concepts**: the rules, definitions and frameworks you need, written as short teaching notes.
**Exam traps**: the distinctions that most often separate a right answer from a tempting wrong one.
**Remember**: a few lines to review the night before.

blocks.text: Practice questions with explanations, the case studies, a glossary and the numbers worth memorizing each have their own page.

**Who it is for.** Engineers-in-training, geoscientists-in-training and internationally trained engineers applying to a Canadian regulator. Examples lean towards process and chemical engineering, but the law and ethics apply to every discipline.

**One national exam, many regulators.** The NPPE is written by candidates in most provinces and territories, so questions use principles common to all of them. Learn the shared principles; do not memorize one province's Act, bylaws or code word for word. Where British Columbia differs or adds a requirement, a short "BC note" points it out.
**Not legal advice.** This is a study resource. Laws, fees and exam rules change: confirm anything you will rely on with your regulator, the official NPPE website and the statute itself.

The NPPE is a closed-book, computer-based exam of 110 multiple-choice questions in 2.5 hours, and you pass with a scaled score of 65. It tests professionalism, ethics, professional practice and law, not technical engineering.

Scaled score of 65, set by the modified-Angoff method and equated between sessions. A scaled 65 is not the same as 65 % correct

One optional break; the timer keeps running
Five a year. 2026 sessions: 19–21 January, 30 March–1 April, 8–10 June, 17–19 August, 2–4 November
13 engineering and geoscience regulators. Quebec's Ordre des ingénieurs du Québec runs its own process

You are exempt from the NPPE if you have already passed a professional practice exam with another Canadian regulator.

lead.text: Four weeks at 6–8 hours a week is enough for most candidates, provided you study to the blueprint rather than reading the textbooks cover to cover. The commonest mistake is spending days on low-weight material (the full CIPO guides, a provincial OH&S manual) while under-practising ethics scenarios and contract law.

pages.title: How to answer NPPE questions

lead.text: Most NPPE questions have two plausible answers; the right one is the one a careful, law-abiding professional would choose first. Common sense gets you close, but the exam rewards a few consistent rules.

items.text: **Public safety comes first.** When safety, health or the environment is at risk, that duty outranks duties to an employer, a client, a colleague or yourself, including confidentiality.

**Fix it at the lowest effective level first.** Verify the facts, raise the concern with the person responsible, then escalate inside the organization in writing. Go to the regulator or authorities when internal routes fail or danger is imminent.
**Disclose, then decide.** For a conflict of interest, disclose it to everyone affected and get informed consent. If the conflict could corrupt your judgment, step aside.
**Stay within your competence.** Decline, get training, or bring in a qualified specialist. Never seal work you are not competent to judge.
**Seal only what you prepared or truly supervised and reviewed.** A seal accepts responsibility; it is not a formality or a favour.
**Law questions are answered with the law.** Apply the legal rule (offer and acceptance, the elements of negligence, limitation periods), not what feels fair.
**Discipline is for registrants; enforcement is for non-registrants.** A regulator disciplines its members and prosecutes or seeks injunctions against unlicensed people.
**Pick the best answer, not a true one.** Several options may be true statements. Choose the one that answers the question asked, most completely.
**Be wary of absolutes and extremes.** Options with "always", "never", "immediately call the media" or "resign at once" are usually wrong.
**Use only the facts given.** Do not invent a contract term, a provincial rule or a motive the question does not state.

subsections.title: The escalation ladder for a safety concern

items.text: Confirm the facts and your own understanding; consult a qualified colleague if needed.
Raise it with the person directly responsible and propose a solution.
Put it in writing to your supervisor, then to senior management.
If unresolved and the risk is real, report to the regulator or the relevant authority (for example the OH&S regulator or the building official).
Going public, or resigning in protest, are last resorts; resigning alone rarely protects the public.

blocks.text: If harm is imminent, skip ahead: warn those at risk and notify the authority immediately.

pages.title: Professionalism

lead.text: A profession is a self-regulated group whose specialized knowledge is used for the public good; the public grants it exclusive rights in return for protecting the public. Expect 7–10 questions.

**Blueprint topics:** definition of professionalism and professional status; roles and responsibilities of professionals in society; the engineering and geoscience professions in Canada and their scopes of practice; the value of the professions to society.

blocks.text: A useful test is to ask who sets the rules, who checks the work, and whom the work is ultimately for.

rows: Training or certification, often set by an employer or industry body
Accredited degree, supervised experience, a law and ethics exam, then a licence granted under statute
Who sets and enforces the standards?
The profession itself, through a regulator the legislature created
The public first, then clients and employers, the regulator and the courts
What happens if you fall short?
You may lose the job or the customer
You can be disciplined, restricted or lose the right to practise
No; keeping competent is a continuing duty

blocks.text: Regulating professions is a provincial and territorial power. Each legislature passes an Act (in BC, the *Professional Governance Act* with an engineers and geoscientists regulation) that creates a regulator and delegates the work of regulation to it.

items.text: The regulator's mandate is to **protect the public interest**, not to promote its members. Advocacy for members, where it exists, is done by separate bodies.
A **council** governs the regulator. Most councillors are registrants elected by registrants; a minority are **public (lay) members**, usually appointed by government, who add an outside view.
The regulator is funded mainly by registrants' fees, not by taxpayers.
Self-regulation gives two exclusive rights:
**Right to title**: only registrants may use "Professional Engineer", "P.Eng.", "Professional Geoscientist", "P.Geo." and, generally, "engineer" in a professional sense.
**Right to practise**: only registrants (and permitted firms) may practise within the legal scope of practice.

The privilege can be taken away. A legislature can tighten or remove self-regulation at any time. BC, for example, replaced its engineering Act with the *Professional Governance Act* in 2021 after a government review of professional reliance, adding regulation of firms and a statutory duty to report.

blocks.text: Each Act defines the practice of engineering in its own words, but the definitions share three elements. Engineers Canada's model definition describes acts of planning, designing, composing, evaluating, advising, reporting, directing or supervising (or managing any of them) that:

items.text: require the application of engineering principles, and
concern the safeguarding of life, health, property, economic interests, the public welfare or the environment.

blocks.text: Both parts must be present. Running a standard lab test from a written procedure is not engineering; designing the structural support for a public viewing platform clearly is.

rows: Provincial and territorial regulators (EGBC, APEGA, PEO, and others)
License individuals (and in some provinces firms), discipline, enforce the Act

Federation of the 12 engineering regulators; accredits undergraduate programs through the Canadian Engineering Accreditation Board; publishes national guidelines; runs the secondary liability insurance program
Technical societies (CSChE, EIC, CSCE, CIM, IEEE)
Share technical knowledge, run conferences and journals

items.text: The public cannot judge most engineering work for itself, so it relies on the licence as a signal that the work is sound. Every visible failure weakens that signal for all registrants.

Exclusive rights invite suspicion that a profession protects its members rather than the public. The answer is conduct: transparent discipline, honest public statements, and refusing work you are not qualified to do.
Modern projects are multidisciplinary. Knowing where your competence ends, and bringing in others, is now part of professional judgment.
Most engineers are employees. Loyalty to the employer is real, but on safety and ethics your professional judgment is your own and cannot be overruled by a manager.
A new graduate is **not** an engineer in the legal sense and may not use "engineer" or "EIT" until registered with a regulator.
"Holding out" means presenting yourself as licensed when you are not. It is an offence even if you never practise.
Engineers Canada and technical societies **do not** license or discipline anyone.
Public members on council are **not** registrants.
Profession = specialized knowledge + self-regulation + public service + lifelong learning.
Exclusive rights (title and practice) exist to protect the public, not to benefit members.
Practice = engineering principles applied + something worth safeguarding.

pages.title: Ethics

lead.text: Ethics questions test whether you can apply a code of ethics to a realistic dilemma, and the answer almost always starts from the duty to the public. Expect 17–21 questions.

**Blueprint topics:** the role of ethics in society, cultures and customs; classical and modern ethical theories; codes of ethics of Canadian engineers and geoscientists; ethical standards and how they relate to conduct; common dilemmas and making ethical decisions.

items.text: **Morals** are personal beliefs about right and wrong, shaped by culture and upbringing.
**Ethics** is the reasoned study of right conduct; **professional ethics** is the agreed standard for a profession, written down as a code.

**Law** is the minimum society enforces. Something can be legal and still unethical (an undisclosed conflict of interest that breaks no statute), and the code can be enforced through discipline even where no law is broken.

Customs differ across cultures. Working abroad does not suspend your code: a bribe that is "customary" elsewhere is still unethical, and paying a foreign official is an offence under Canada's *Corruption of Foreign Public Officials Act*.

blocks.text: No theory is superior; each gives a different lens. The exam asks you to recognize which theory an argument uses and where it falls short.

rows: It produces the greatest good for the greatest number
Can justify harming a minority; benefits are hard to measure and compare
It follows a duty you would accept as a universal rule, and treats people as ends, never merely as means
Duties can conflict; ignores outcomes; allows no "white lie"
It respects everyone's fundamental rights (life, liberty, property, dignity)
One person's rights can collide with another's
It reflects good character: the "golden mean" between two extremes (courage between cowardice and recklessness)
Vague and hard to apply to a specific decision

blocks.text: The Golden Rule (treat others as you would want to be treated) is consistent with all four. A strong exam answer is one that more than one theory supports.

subsections.title: What every Canadian code of ethics says

blocks.text: Each regulator has its own code, but Engineers Canada's *Guideline on the Code of Ethics* (updated July 2024) synthesizes the common ground. The themes:

rows: Hold their safety, health and welfare **paramount**; protect the environment; promote workplace health and safety
Practise only within your competence, carefully and in line with the law; keep your knowledge current
Act as a faithful agent; keep confidences; avoid conflicts of interest and disclose any that arise; explain the consequences if your judgment is overruled
Integrity, fairness and courtesy; give credit; give and accept honest professional comment; uphold the profession's reputation
Explain engineering issues to the public objectively and truthfully; report hazardous, illegal or unethical practice to the regulator or the proper authority
Treat people fairly and promote equity, diversity and inclusion

blocks.text: "Paramount" means that when public safety or the environment is at stake, every other duty in the code gives way to it.
A conflict of interest exists when a personal, financial or other interest could influence, or appear to influence, your professional judgment for someone who relies on you.

items.text: **Actual, potential or perceived:** all three matter. A perceived conflict damages trust even when your judgment was sound.

**Typical examples:** owning shares in a supplier you recommend; reviewing a design for a regulator that your own firm prepared; accepting gifts or hospitality from a contractor whose claim you assess; moonlighting for a competitor or a client of your employer; hiring a relative (nepotism); being paid by both sides of a deal.
**Work through three questions:**
Can the interest be removed (sell the shares, hand the file to someone else)? If so, remove it.
If not, have you told everyone affected, in writing, and do they agree you should continue?
Even with their agreement, could the interest still bend the judgment they rely on? If yes, step aside or have an independent party decide.
**Moonlighting** is allowed if your employer knows, you use none of its time, equipment or confidential information, and you do not compete with it.

blocks.text: Ask these questions in order. They work on the exam and at work.

items.text: **What do I actually know?** Separate facts from assumptions, and note who could be harmed.
**Whose interests collide?** Name the duties in tension: public, client, employer, colleague, yourself.
**What are all my options?** Exam scenarios often offer two extremes. There is usually a middle route, such as raising the concern in writing or proposing a safer design.
**How does each option hold up?** Test it against the law, your code of ethics, and the four theories. An option that several tests support is the strong one.
**What will I do, and how will I record it?** Act, keep a written record, and check that the problem was actually resolved.

subsections.title: Common dilemmas and the expected response

rows: Your technical recommendation is overruled, and there is no safety risk
Make your recommendation and its consequences clear in writing, then accept the decision
Your recommendation is overruled and the public is at risk
Refuse to proceed; escalate in writing; report to the regulator or authority if not resolved
You are asked to do something illegal or against the code
Refuse, explain why, and offer a lawful alternative
You find a serious error in a colleague's work
Tell the colleague first; if it is not corrected and the risk is real, escalate
A client asks you to review another engineer's work
Notify that engineer that you are reviewing it (unless they have left the project or it is a legal review); do not supplant them by undercutting
A supplier offers you a holiday
Decline; modest token hospitality only within your employer's policy
Confidential client information reveals a danger to the public
Public safety overrides confidentiality: raise it with the client, then report if needed
You are asked to work outside your competence
Decline, or accept only with a competent specialist or mentor and with the client informed

items.text: The duty to the public is **paramount**, not merely "first among equals".
"Report to the media" is almost never the first correct step.
Disclosure alone is not always enough; informed consent, or withdrawal, may be needed.
An ethical duty can exist without a legal duty, and vice versa.

Identify the theory from its reasoning: "most people benefit" is utilitarian; "I must never lie" is Kantian duty; "they have a right to know" is rights ethics; "what would a person of good character do" is virtue ethics.
Public safety and the environment first, then competence, then faithful service to clients and employers.
Conflicts: avoid, disclose with consent, or withdraw.
Mill = consequences; Kant = duty; Locke = rights; Aristotle = virtue and the golden mean.

pages.title: Professional Practice

lead.text: Professional Practice is the largest area of the exam (27–32 questions) and asks how a careful professional behaves day to day: what standard you are held to, what you may seal, how you manage risk, and what to do when something is wrong.

**Blueprint topics:** accountability, workplace issues and standards of practice; responsibilities to employers and clients; relations with other professionals and non-professionals; statutory and non-statutory standards; risk, insurance, quality management and due diligence; environmental responsibility and sustainable development; software and computer tools; documentation authentication and control; duty to inform and whistleblowing; communication.

subsections.title: III.1 Accountability and the standard of care

items.text: The **standard of care** is that of a reasonably competent practitioner in the same field, in the same circumstances, at the time. It is not perfection, and it is not the standard of the best expert in the country.

Following the codes, standards and your regulator's practice guidelines is strong evidence that you met the standard of care, but it is not a complete defence if a reasonable engineer would have done more.

**Supervision:** trainees (EIT, GIT) and non-registrants may do engineering work only under the direct supervision of a registrant, who reviews it and takes professional responsibility for it. Accountability is shared, but the registrant who seals is responsible for the sealed work.
**Competence** is personal and specific. A P.Eng. in process design is not automatically competent to design a pressure-vessel support structure.
A professional employee is personally responsible for their professional work, even when the employer is also liable.

subsections.title: III.2 Clients, employers and other professionals

items.text: **Faithful agent:** act in the client's or employer's interest, within the law and the code; keep their information confidential, except where public safety requires otherwise.
**Written agreements:** define scope, deliverables, fees, schedule, limits of liability and who owns the documents. Most disputes start with an unclear scope.

**Work product:** documents created by an employee in the course of employment generally belong to the employer, including copyright. A consultant's documents belong to the consultant unless the contract says otherwise; the client usually receives a licence to use them for that project.

**Selecting engineers:** qualifications-based selection (choose the best-qualified firm, then negotiate the fee) is recommended for professional services. Fee competition is not unethical in itself, but cutting the fee must never cut the quality or safety of the work.
**Other professionals:** respect their areas of competence (architects, geoscientists, technologists, lawyers); do not review or supplant another engineer's work without notifying them.

blocks.text: Management theory occasionally appears. Douglas McGregor contrasted two views of employees: **Theory X** treats them as needing close control and external motivation, while **Theory Y** treats them as self-motivated people who seek responsibility. Engineers who supervise others are expected to delegate clearly and remain accountable for the work they approve.

rows: Provincial building and fire codes, OH&S regulations, pressure-equipment and electrical safety regulations, environmental regulations
National Building Code, National Fire Code (published by the National Research Council)
None until a province, territory or municipality adopts them, with or without amendments
CSA, ASTM, ASME, API, ISO, NFPA, company standards
Voluntary, unless a law or a contract references them, which makes them binding

blocks.text: The Standards Council of Canada accredits standards-development organizations such as CSA Group. Courts treat recognized standards as the minimum acceptable practice.

Codes and standards are a floor, not a ceiling. A design can comply with every clause and still be unsafe in a situation the code writers did not foresee, so a reasonable engineer also asks what could go wrong in this particular use, and designs it out where possible.

subsections.title: III.4 Risk, insurance, quality and due diligence

blocks.text: **Risk** is the combination of likelihood and consequence. A qualitative assessment ranks each risk on a probability × severity matrix.

rows: Re-route a pipeline away from a slope
Add a relief valve, redundancy, inspection
Shift the financial consequence to someone else

items.text: **Hierarchy of controls** for workplace hazards: elimination, substitution, engineering controls, administrative controls, personal protective equipment.
**Prevention over detection:** it is cheaper and safer to design a failure out than to find and fix it later.
**Risk–utility analysis** asks whether a product's usefulness justifies its foreseeable hazards; it is how courts judge design defects.

blocks.text: Insurance and bonds

rows: Usually *claims-made*: the policy in force when the claim is made responds, so you need run-off cover after you stop practising
Third-party bodily injury and property damage from operations
Claims against a company's directors and officers
Individual registrants when no other insurance responds
$250,000 plus defence costs, includes whistleblowing support; covers individuals, not firms; automatic in participating regulators including EGBC, APEGA and APEGS
Owner, if the low bidder refuses to sign the contract
Owner, if the contractor fails to complete the work
Subcontractors and suppliers who go unpaid

blocks.text: A **certificate of insurance** is only evidence that a policy existed on a date; the policy wording governs.

**Quality management:** ISO 9001 sets requirements for a quality management system; ISO 14001 for an environmental management system; ISO 45001 for an occupational health and safety system. Quality assurance is the planned system that prevents errors; quality control is the checking that finds them.

**Due diligence** means taking all reasonable care in the circumstances. For regulatory "strict liability" offences (most OH&S and environmental offences), a defendant who proves due diligence on a balance of probabilities avoids conviction. Keep records that show it: training, inspections, procedures, corrective actions.

subsections.title: III.5 Environmental responsibility and sustainable development

items.text: Codes now pair the environment with public safety as a paramount duty.
**Sustainable development** meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs (the Brundtland Commission's definition, 1987).

**At the start of a project:** identify the environmental laws, permits and affected communities; bring in specialists such as hydrogeologists or biologists where the questions are outside your field.

**While designing:** compare options over their whole life cycle, including energy, emissions, waste and closure costs, not only capital cost. Where harm could be serious or irreversible, lack of full certainty is not a reason to delay protective measures (the precautionary principle).
**When things go wrong:** tell the people who need to know, including the regulator where the law requires it, and fix the cause rather than the symptom.
**Climate:** practice guidelines increasingly expect engineers to consider climate-change adaptation (future loads, floods, heat) and emissions in design.

**Indigenous engagement:** the duty to consult Indigenous peoples belongs to the Crown, but engineers support it through early, respectful engagement. BC has legislated the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (DRIPA, 2019).

subsections.title: III.6 Software, computers and online tools

items.text: The professional, not the software vendor, is responsible for results used in their work.

Understand the program's theory, assumptions and limits; validate it against hand calculations, known solutions or test data; check that inputs are right and outputs are reasonable; record the version used.
Use only properly licensed software.
The same applies to AI tools and online calculators: you may use them, but you must verify the output and you remain accountable for it.

subsections.title: III.7 Authenticating documents: seals and stamps

items.text: Applying your seal, signature and date means you accept professional responsibility for the document. It is **not** a guarantee that the work is free of error.
Seal only documents you prepared, or that were prepared under your direct supervision, or that you reviewed thoroughly enough to accept full responsibility.
Seal final documents issued for use by others: drawings, specifications, reports, calculations, field reviews. Mark drafts "Preliminary" or "Not for construction" instead of sealing them.
Never seal another person's work as a favour, lend your seal, or let others apply it. Never seal work outside your competence.
A sealed document changed after issue must be revised and re-authenticated by a registrant who accepts responsibility for the change.
Electronic seals are acceptable when the method is secure and the document is protected from alteration.
Firms need a **permit to practice** (called a certificate of authorization in some provinces), and some regulators require the firm's permit number on authenticated documents.

subsections.title: III.8 Duty to inform and whistleblowing

items.text: **Whistleblowing** is disclosing, to an outside authority, wrongdoing by your own organization that threatens the public.
It is justified when the harm is serious, you have checked your facts, you have tried internal routes (unless danger is imminent), and disclosure is likely to prevent the harm.

Protections: OH&S laws prohibit reprisal against workers who raise safety concerns; the *Criminal Code* makes it an offence for an employer to retaliate against an employee who reports an offence to law enforcement; the secondary insurance program helps with legal costs.

**BC note:** section 58 of the *Professional Governance Act* creates a **statutory** duty for registrants to report to a regulator when they have reasonable and probable grounds to believe another registrant's practice may pose a risk of significant harm. Section 103 prohibits reprisals against anyone who reports.
Write so the reader can act: state the purpose, findings, recommendations, assumptions and limitations.
Put important advice in writing, especially when it is not followed; keep minutes and a decision record.
Speak to the public objectively and within your competence. Separate facts from opinions, and do not comment publicly on another professional's work without knowing the facts.
Letters of reference must be honest; an inflated reference can mislead a regulator or employer.
Standard of care is the *reasonable* practitioner, not the best one.
A seal is acceptance of responsibility, not a warranty.
The National Building Code alone has no legal force.
CGL insurance does not cover professional negligence.
Professional liability insurance is usually claims-made, not occurrence-based.
"Transfer" (insurance, fixed price) is a risk response; "mitigate" reduces the risk itself.
Seal only what you prepared, supervised or fully reviewed, and only within your competence.
Avoid, reduce, transfer, accept.
Verify software; you own the result.
Escalate internally first, in writing; report externally when that fails or danger is imminent.

lead.text: Law is the second-largest area (23–28 questions), and contracts and torts carry most of it. Learn the elements and the remedies; the exam tests whether you can apply a rule to a short fact pattern.

**Blueprint topics:** the Canadian legal system; contract law; tort law; civil law in Quebec; business, employment and labour law; dispute resolution; intellectual property; expert witnesses; bonds and construction liens; international law; environmental law; workers' compensation and OH&S; human rights and privacy.

items.text: **Constitution:** the *Constitution Act, 1867* divides powers. Parliament has criminal law, patents, copyright, banking, trade and commerce, and federal works. Provinces have property and civil rights (contracts, torts, employment), municipal matters and the regulation of professions. The *Charter of Rights and Freedoms* (1982) limits what both may do.

**Sources of law:** statutes and regulations made by legislatures, and the **common law**, made by judges through **precedent** (*stare decisis*): lower courts must follow higher courts' decisions on similar facts.

**Courts:** provincial courts; superior trial courts (the Supreme Court of British Columbia, the Ontario Superior Court of Justice); provincial courts of appeal; the Supreme Court of Canada at the top. The Federal Court hears federal matters such as patents and trademarks.
**Administrative tribunals** (a regulator's discipline committee, a labour board) decide under a statute and are reviewed by the courts.

rows: Punish and deter conduct harmful to society
Balance of probabilities (more likely than not)

blocks.text: Between the two sit **regulatory (quasi-criminal) offences** under OH&S and environmental statutes. Most are **strict liability**: the Crown proves the act, and the defendant escapes conviction only by proving due diligence. Professional discipline is a separate proceeding again; the rule against double jeopardy does not stop a regulator disciplining a registrant who has also been convicted or sued for the same conduct.
A contract is an agreement the courts will enforce. It can be oral, written or implied by conduct, though some contracts (for example for land) must be in writing.
Elements of a valid contract

items.text: **Offer and acceptance:** a clear offer, accepted unconditionally.
**Consideration:** each side gives something of value. Past consideration does not count; a document under seal needs none.
**Intention to create legal relations:** presumed in business dealings.
**Capacity:** minors, people lacking mental capacity and the seriously intoxicated may avoid a contract.
**Legality:** a contract for an illegal purpose is void.

blocks.text: Offer and acceptance rules

items.text: An advertisement or a call for tenders is usually an *invitation to treat*, not an offer. A **bid is an offer**.
A counter-offer rejects the original offer.
An offer can be revoked any time before acceptance, but revocation takes effect only when received.
Acceptance must be communicated; silence is not acceptance.

**Postal acceptance rule:** an acceptance sent by mail is effective when posted. The rule applies only to acceptances; offers, revocations and rejections take effect on receipt. Instant communication (email, phone) takes effect on receipt.
A **letter of intent** is usually not binding unless the parties show they intended to be bound.

blocks.text: Tendering: Contract A and Contract B

items.text: Under *R. v. Ron Engineering* (Supreme Court of Canada, 1981), submitting a compliant bid creates **Contract A** between owner and bidder. Its terms come from the tender documents: typically the bid cannot be withdrawn before it is accepted or the validity period ends, and the bid deposit can be forfeited.
Awarding the work forms **Contract B**, the construction contract itself.

*M.J.B. Enterprises v. Defence Construction* (1999): a "lowest or any tender not necessarily accepted" privilege clause does not let the owner accept a **non-compliant** bid; the owner owes compliant bidders fair and equal treatment.
*Tercon Contractors v. British Columbia* (2010): accepting an ineligible bidder breached Contract A, and the exclusion clause did not protect the owner.

blocks.text: Terms and interpretation

items.text: Courts look for the parties' objective intention, reading the words in context.
**Contra proferentem:** an ambiguous term is read against the party who drafted it.
**Parol evidence rule:** evidence of earlier oral or written agreements cannot contradict a complete written contract. An *entire agreement* clause reinforces this.
**Conditions** are essential terms; breach lets the innocent party end the contract. **Warranties** are minor; breach gives damages only. "Time is of the essence" makes deadlines conditions.

**Privity:** only parties can enforce or be bound by a contract, with exceptions such as agency, assignment and some third-party beneficiaries (employees protected by a contractual limitation clause).
**Assignment:** contractual *rights* can usually be assigned; personal services and *obligations* cannot be transferred without the other party's consent.

**Good faith:** every contract carries a duty of honest performance (*Bhasin v. Hrynew*, 2014); a party may not knowingly mislead the other (*C.M. Callow v. Zollinger*, 2020), and contractual discretion must be exercised reasonably (*Wastech v. Greater Vancouver Sewerage and Drainage District*, 2021).

Mistake: a shared, fundamental mistake made before agreement

Frustration: an unforeseen event, not caused by either party, makes performance impossible or radically different
Contract ends; neither party is liable for future performance

blocks.text: A **force majeure** clause allocates in advance the risk of events beyond the parties' control (storms, war, strikes, pandemics).
Ending a contract

items.text: **Performance**, the usual way.
**Agreement** (mutual release, or substituting a new contract).
**Frustration.**

**Breach:** a fundamental breach or a **repudiation** (words or conduct showing a party will not perform) lets the innocent party end the contract and claim damages. An **anticipatory breach** is a repudiation before performance is due.
A **termination clause** sets agreed grounds and notice. Insolvency of a party is a common express ground.

blocks.text: Remedies for breach

rows: Put the innocent party where it would have been had the contract been performed
A genuine pre-estimate of loss stated in the contract (for example a daily amount for late completion); a sum that is really a penalty is not enforced
Court orders performance where damages are inadequate (unique goods, land); not for personal services
Court orders a party to stop (or do) something
Reasonable payment for work done where there is no enforceable contract or price

blocks.text: Damages are limited by three rules: the loss must not be too **remote** (it must have been in the parties' reasonable contemplation when they contracted, *Hadley v. Baxendale*); the innocent party must **mitigate**; and losses must be proven, not **speculative**.

**Exclusion and limitation of liability clauses** are enforced if they apply to the breach on a fair reading, were not unconscionable when made, and no overriding public policy defeats them (*Tercon*, 2010).
Construction contracts and delivery methods

items.text: Standard forms come from the Canadian Construction Documents Committee (CCDC): CCDC 2 (stipulated price), CCDC 3 (cost plus), CCDC 4 (unit price), CCDC 5A/5B (construction management), CCDC 14/15 (design-build). Consultant agreements commonly use ACEC Document 31.
Under CCDC contracts the consultant acts for the owner as its agent, and must also act impartially when interpreting the contract and certifying payments.
A **change order** is a signed agreement adjusting scope, price or time; a **change directive** instructs a change before the price is agreed. Additions are *extras*, reductions are *credits*.

One contract for design and construction; work can start before design is complete
Construction manager advises during design, then builds to a guaranteed maximum price
Private partner designs, builds, finances and operates for a concession period

blocks.text: **Performance specifications** state the result required and leave the method to the contractor; **prescriptive specifications** state the method and materials, so the owner carries more risk if they fail.

A tort is a civil wrong, other than a breach of contract, for which the courts award compensation. Its aim is to compensate the victim, not punish the wrongdoer. Liability in contract and tort can exist at the same time (**concurrent liability**, *Central Trust v. Rafuse*, 1986; *BG Checo v. BC Hydro*, 1993).

rows: Careless design, negligent misrepresentation, careless inspection
Escape of a dangerous thing from land (*Rylands v. Fletcher*)

blocks.text: **Elements of negligence** (all must be proved by the plaintiff on a balance of probabilities):

items.text: **Duty of care:** the defendant owed the plaintiff a duty, because harm was reasonably foreseeable and the relationship was close enough (*Donoghue v. Stevenson*'s "neighbour" principle; in Canada the *Anns/Cooper* test).
**Breach:** the defendant fell below the standard of a reasonable person, or for a professional, a reasonably competent professional.
**Causation:** the breach caused the loss, usually on the "but for" test.
**Remoteness:** the type of harm was a reasonably foreseeable consequence (*Mustapha v. Culligan*, 2008).
**Damage:** actual loss or injury.

blocks.text: Cases engineers should know

items.text: **Negligent misrepresentation:** a careless statement relied on by someone the speaker should have expected to rely on it (*Hedley Byrne*, 1963; *Queen v. Cognos*, 1993). Opinions and reports are a common source of claims.

***Edgeworth Construction v. N.D. Lea*** (1993): an engineering firm that prepared tender drawings and specifications owed a duty of care to a contractor who relied on them, although the contractor had no contract with the firm.
***Winnipeg Condominium v. Bird Construction*** (1995): a builder (and by extension designers) can be liable to later owners for the cost of repairing defects that pose a real danger.

**Personal liability of employees:** a professional employee can be personally liable in tort for their own negligence even though they act for a company (*London Drugs v. Kuehne & Nagel*, 1992), which is why firms' policies should cover their employees.
**Vicarious liability:** an employer is liable for torts its employees commit in the course of employment (*Bazley v. Curry*, 1999), but generally not for an independent contractor.

blocks.text: Other tort ideas that appear in questions

items.text: **Joint and several liability:** two or more tortfeasors who caused the same loss can each be made to pay all of it; they then share contributions among themselves.
**Contributory negligence:** a plaintiff who was partly at fault has damages reduced in proportion.
**Voluntary assumption of risk** (*volenti*): a full defence, rarely successful.

**Res ipsa loquitur** ("the thing speaks for itself"): where an accident would not normally happen without negligence and the defendant controlled the cause. Canada no longer treats it as a separate doctrine (*Fontaine v. BC*, 1998), but the circumstantial reasoning still applies.

**Thin skull rule:** the defendant takes the victim as found and pays for all the harm, even if the victim was unusually vulnerable. **Crumbling skull:** if the condition would have worsened anyway, the defendant pays only for the extra harm (*Athey v. Leonati*, 1996).
**Occupiers' liability:** occupiers owe visitors reasonable care for their safety (provincial statutes).

**Nuisance:** unreasonable interference with a neighbour's use and enjoyment of land (noise, vibration, dust). **Trespass:** entering land without permission; no damage need be proven. A landowner also has a right to lateral support from neighbouring land.

**Defamation:** a false statement that harms reputation. *Libel* is written or recorded; *slander* is spoken. Defences: truth (justification), fair comment, absolute or qualified privilege, responsible communication on matters of public interest.
**Punitive damages** punish outrageous conduct and are rare.

blocks.text: **Limitation periods** set deadlines to sue. Most provinces use a basic period from the date the claim was **discovered** (or ought to have been) and an ultimate period from the act itself.

items.text: Quebec's private law (contracts, property, liability) is governed by the **Civil Code of Québec** (in force 1994), descended from the French civil law tradition. The rest of Canada uses English **common law**.
In the civil law the code is the primary source; judges interpret it, and earlier decisions are persuasive rather than binding.
Federal law (criminal law, patents, copyright, bankruptcy) applies in Quebec as everywhere else.
Terms differ: "extra-contractual liability" is the civil law counterpart of tort.

Under the Civil Code, the contractor, architect and engineer who took part in a building's construction are jointly (*solidarily*) liable for its loss within **five years** of completion, unless they prove an exemption (for example that a decision imposed by the client caused the loss).
Engineers in Quebec are regulated by the Ordre des ingénieurs du Québec, which sets its own professional practice exam.

blocks.text: Incorporating does **not** shield a professional from personal liability for their own negligent professional work.

A **fiduciary** must act in the best interests of the person relying on them, avoid conflicts and not profit secretly. Directors, officers, agents and trustees are fiduciaries; senior employees can be too. **Insider trading**, buying or selling securities using material non-public information or tipping others, is an offence.
Employment law

items.text: Employment is a contract, with terms implied by law: the employee's duties of **fidelity** (loyalty, confidentiality, no competing while employed) and **competence**, and the employer's duty to give **reasonable notice** of termination without cause.

**Dismissal for just cause** (serious misconduct, dishonesty, wilful disobedience) needs no notice. Without cause, the employer must give reasonable notice or pay in lieu, never less than the provincial employment standards minimum. Courts set reasonable notice from age, length of service, the type of job and the availability of similar work.
**Constructive dismissal:** a unilateral, fundamental change to the job (pay cut, demotion) can be treated as dismissal.

**Restrictive covenants** (non-competition, non-solicitation) are enforced only if reasonable in time, geography and scope; a non-solicitation clause is easier to enforce than a non-competition clause. Ontario has banned most non-competition clauses in employment since 2021.

**Employee or contractor?** Courts look at control, ownership of tools, chance of profit and risk of loss, and how integrated the worker is into the business (*671122 Ontario v. Sagaz*, 2001). A "contractor" who works only for one firm, under its direction, is likely an employee in law.

**Labour law** governs unionized workplaces: certification of a union by a labour relations board, collective bargaining, a collective agreement, and grievances decided by arbitration rather than courts. Strikes and lockouts are not allowed while a collective agreement is in force.

Used in construction (prompt payment laws) so work continues; can be revisited later

items.text: **International commercial arbitration** is governed by provincial international commercial arbitration acts and, for federal matters, the federal *Commercial Arbitration Act*. All are based on the UNCITRAL Model Law.

Arbitration and mediation suit parties who want privacy (trade secrets) or an ongoing relationship. They suit poorly cases needing court orders against third parties, urgent injunctions, or where the power imbalance is large.

**Litigation vocabulary:** *pleadings* are the documents that set out each side's case (statement of claim, defence, reply). *Discovery of documents* is the exchange of relevant documents. *Examination for discovery* is the oral questioning of the other party under oath before trial; *interrogatories* are written questions. A **without prejudice** (settlement-privileged) offer cannot be used as evidence if the negotiation fails.

blocks.text: Intellectual property is federal law, administered by the Canadian Intellectual Property Office (CIPO). Learn what each right protects, how long it lasts and how disclosure affects it.

blocks.text: Patents

items.text: Not patentable: scientific principles, abstract theorems and mathematical formulas, mere ideas, methods of medical treatment, and higher life forms (whole plants and animals). Lower life forms such as bacteria and cell lines can be patented.

Canada is first-to-file. Disclosing the invention before filing destroys novelty in most countries. Canada and the US give the applicant a **12-month grace period** after their own disclosure; Europe gives none.
Applications are published 18 months after filing (or priority date). After grant, the owner can claim reasonable compensation for use since publication, and is responsible for enforcing the patent.

**Paris Convention priority:** file elsewhere within 12 months of the first filing (6 months for trademarks and industrial designs) and keep the first filing date. The **Patent Cooperation Treaty** lets one international application start the process in many countries.
"Patent pending" marking is optional, but marking falsely is an offence.

Unlike copyright, there is no general Canadian statute giving employers an employee's inventions. Ownership follows the employment contract, or whether the employee was hired to invent; clear IP clauses avoid disputes.
A *divisional* application claims a separate invention that was disclosed but not claimed in an earlier "parent" application.

blocks.text: Trademarks

items.text: Since 17 June 2019, use is no longer required to register, and terms are 10 years (previously 15).
After three years of registration, a mark that has not been used in Canada can be expunged (section 45 of the *Trademarks Act*).
Canada joined the Madrid Protocol in 2019: one international application can cover many countries.
A **certification mark** shows that goods meet a defined standard.
The ® and ™ symbols are not required in Canada.

blocks.text: Copyright

items.text: Only the expression is protected, not the idea, the method or the data.

The general term became life plus 70 years on 30 December 2022; works already in the public domain did not regain protection. For joint works, the term runs from the death of the last surviving author.
**Crown copyright** (government works) lasts 50 years from the end of the year of first publication; this did not change in 2022.

**Ownership:** an employee's work made in the course of employment belongs to the employer, unless agreed otherwise. A contractor (freelance consultant) owns the copyright in what they create unless the contract assigns it.
**Moral rights** (attribution, integrity, association) stay with the author; they can be waived but not assigned.
An owner can **assign** copyright (transfer it) or **license** it (permit use while keeping ownership).
**Fair dealing** allows limited use for research, private study, education, parody, satire, criticism, review and news reporting.
Software users may make a backup copy and adapt a program for compatibility with their own computer.

blocks.text: **Trade secrets** are protected by contract (confidentiality agreements) and the law of breach of confidence. Protection ends if the information becomes public, including through independent discovery or reverse engineering. Accepting a competitor's confidential data from its former employee is unethical and may be unlawful.

items.text: An expert gives the court opinion evidence on matters beyond ordinary knowledge. Their **overriding duty is to the court**: to be fair, objective and non-partisan, even though one party hired and pays them (*White Burgess v. Abbott and Haliburton*, 2015).
Stay within your expertise; state your facts, assumptions, methods and limitations; correct your report if your opinion changes.
The expert's report must normally be served on the other side before trial under the court rules (in BC, the Supreme Court Civil Rules).
Never accept a fee that depends on the outcome; it destroys independence.
Witnesses generally have immunity from civil suits for their testimony, but an expert can still be disciplined by their regulator, and the court can reject biased evidence.
A **fact witness** reports only what they saw and did; an engineer can be either.

**Construction (builders') liens** are created by provincial statute. They give those who supply work or materials to improve land a claim against the owner's interest in that land, so the owner cannot sell or refinance freely until the lien is cleared.

**Holdbacks:** the owner (and each contractor down the chain) holds back a percentage of each payment, typically 10 %, so that money is available to pay valid liens. An owner who keeps the holdback is liable only up to that amount.
Liens must be registered within a strict time after completion, and then "perfected" by starting a court action within a further deadline. Late claims are lost.
An owner can clear a lien from title by paying money into court or posting a **lien bond**. Prospective buyers search for liens before closing.
Liens generally cannot be registered against Crown land; other remedies apply there.

items.text: Treaties bind Canada internationally, but they take effect inside Canada only through implementing federal or provincial legislation. Once implemented, governments and procuring bodies must comply (for example with the procurement rules in trade agreements).

Trade and mobility agreements (CUSMA, CETA, the Canadian Free Trade Agreement, the Washington Accord for accredited degrees) ease recognition, but **you must still be licensed where you practise**. A BC engineer sealing drawings for a plant in Washington State needs a Washington licence.
Abroad, you follow local law and your Canadian code of ethics. The *Corruption of Foreign Public Officials Act* makes bribing a foreign official a Canadian offence.

Both levels of government legislate. Federal examples: the *Canadian Environmental Protection Act, 1999*, the *Fisheries Act*, the *Impact Assessment Act*, the *Species at Risk Act*, the *Transportation of Dangerous Goods Act*. Provincial examples in BC: the *Environmental Management Act* and the *Environmental Assessment Act*.
Most environmental offences are strict liability (due diligence is the defence). Directors and officers can be personally liable.

**Polluter pays:** those responsible for contamination pay for remediation. Under BC's contaminated sites regime, past and present owners and operators can be liable even if they did not cause the pollution.

**Environmental site assessments** (CSA standards): Phase I reviews records, interviews and site observations for evidence of contamination; Phase II samples and analyses soil and water; Phase III (or remediation) delineates and cleans up.
**Environmental audits** check compliance and help prove due diligence.

subsections.title: IV.12 Workers' compensation and occupational health and safety

items.text: **Workers' compensation** is provincial, **no-fault** insurance. Injured workers receive benefits regardless of who was at fault; in exchange, they generally cannot sue their employer. Employers pay premiums based on payroll, industry and safety record. In BC the system is run by WorkSafeBC under the *Workers Compensation Act*.

**OH&S legislation** sets minimum safety standards and duties for employers, supervisors, workers, owners and **prime contractors** on multi-employer sites. Breaches are provincial regulatory offences, with due diligence as the defence.
**Workers' three rights:** to *know* about hazards (training, labelling under WHMIS), to *participate* (joint health and safety committees), and to *refuse* unsafe work without reprisal.
The **internal responsibility system** means everyone in the workplace shares responsibility for safety, in proportion to their authority.

**Criminal liability (the Westray law):** after 26 miners died at the Westray mine in Nova Scotia in 1992, Parliament added section 217.1 to the *Criminal Code* (in force 31 March 2004). Anyone who directs how another person works must take reasonable steps to prevent bodily harm; serious failures can lead to criminal negligence charges against individuals and organizations.

**Human rights codes** (provincial; the *Canadian Human Rights Act* for federally regulated employers) prohibit discrimination in employment and services on grounds such as race, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, age and disability.

Employers must **accommodate** to the point of undue hardship. A rule that discriminates is allowed only as a **bona fide occupational requirement**: rationally connected to the job, adopted in good faith, and reasonably necessary, with accommodation impossible without undue hardship (*Meiorin*, 1999).
Employers must prevent and respond to **harassment**; failing to act can make them liable.

**Privacy:** the federal *Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act* (PIPEDA) governs private-sector personal information, except where a province has a substantially similar law (BC and Alberta have their own *Personal Information Protection Act*). Public bodies have separate freedom-of-information laws. Privacy law protects individuals, not corporations.

Core principles: collect only what you need, with consent, for a stated purpose; protect it; let people see their own information. Workplace monitoring must be reasonable and proportionate, and information can be disclosed without consent in emergencies that threaten someone's life or safety.

subsections.title: Other areas of law that appear

items.text: **Competition Act:** bid-rigging (agreeing among bidders who will win) is a criminal offence.
**Criminal Code:** fraud, and secret commissions (paying or accepting a kickback to influence a business decision), are offences.
**Sale of goods acts:** implied conditions that goods match their description and are of merchantable quality and fit for purpose.
A bid is an **offer**; the postal rule applies to acceptances only.
A privilege clause does not let an owner accept a non-compliant bid.
Negligence needs **all** elements; a careless act without damage is not actionable.
Mediators can meet the parties separately and do not impose a decision; arbitrators decide and their award binds.
Copyright belongs to the **employer** for employees and to the **contractor** for independent consultants, unless agreed otherwise.
Crown copyright is still 50 years from publication.
The National Building Code, CSA standards and ISO standards are not law until adopted or referenced.
Workers' compensation is no-fault and replaces the right to sue the employer.
Contract = offer + acceptance + consideration + intention + capacity + legality.
Negligence = duty + breach + causation + remoteness + damage.
Patent 20 years; trademark 10 years renewable; copyright life + 70; industrial design 10/15 years; trade secret as long as secret.
Expert witness: duty to the court, no contingency fee.

pages.title: Professional Law

lead.text: Professional law is the legal framework that creates and runs the regulators: who may be licensed, what is reserved to registrants, and how unlicensed practice is stopped. Expect 7–10 questions, asked in general terms rather than about one province's Act.

**Blueprint topics:** the Acts, regulations and bylaws of provincial and territorial regulators; admission to the professions; illegal practice, enforcement against unlicensed practice and misuse of title; professional and technical societies.

blocks.text: The purpose of every Act is to protect the public. **BC note:** since 5 February 2021 the *Professional Governance Act* governs EGBC alongside other regulated professions (agrologists, forest professionals, applied biologists, applied science technologists and architects), overseen by the Office of the Superintendent of Professional Governance; EGBC's code of ethics sits in its bylaws.
The requirements are broadly the same across Canada:

items.text: **Academic:** a CEAB-accredited engineering degree (or Geoscientists Canada standard for geoscience), or an equivalent qualification confirmed by assessment or technical exams.
**Experience:** usually four years of acceptable engineering or geoscience experience, increasingly assessed by competencies rather than by a fixed amount of Canadian experience.
**Professional practice knowledge:** pass the NPPE (and in BC, the online seminar).
**Good character:** honesty and integrity; past discipline or relevant convictions are considered.
**Language:** competence in English (or French where applicable).

Internationally, the Washington Accord recognizes accredited degrees between member countries, but each country still licenses its own practitioners.

subsections.title: Unlicensed practice and misuse of title

items.text: **Unlicensed practice:** a person or firm doing reserved engineering or geoscience work without a licence or permit.

**Misuse of title (holding out):** using "P.Eng.", "Professional Engineer", "engineer" in a way that implies licensure, or "engineering" in a business name, without authorization, even if no engineering is done.

Regulators respond with **enforcement**: warning letters, prosecution in provincial court for an offence under the Act (fines, with higher fines for repeat offences), and **injunctions** from a superior court to stop ongoing unlawful practice. Disobeying an injunction is contempt of court.
**Enforcement** targets non-registrants; **discipline** targets registrants.
Bylaws cannot override the Act.
An EIT cannot take professional responsibility or seal.
Enforcement is not discipline.
A technical society's code of ethics does not replace the regulator's.
Act > regulations > bylaws.
Licence = education + experience + NPPE + character + language.
Title and practice are both protected; misuse of either is an offence.

pages.title: Regulation and Discipline

lead.text: Regulators protect the public after licensing through complaints and discipline, practice reviews, firm regulation and continuing professional development. Expect 7–10 questions.
**Blueprint topics:** discipline procedures; practice reviews of individuals; practice reviews of firms; continuing professional development.

items.text: **Complaint.** Anyone can complain in writing: a client, a member of the public, another registrant, an employer, or the regulator itself (for example the registrar acting on a news report).
**Screening and investigation.** An investigation committee gathers evidence, often with an independent peer reviewer, and gives the registrant a chance to respond.

**Outcome of the investigation.** The committee may dismiss the complaint, resolve it informally (advice, education, mediation), agree a **consent order** in which the registrant admits the conduct and accepts a penalty, or refer it to a hearing.

**Discipline hearing.** A panel of the discipline committee (registrants and a public member) hears evidence. The regulator must prove the case on a **balance of probabilities**. The registrant has the right to notice, to counsel, to present evidence and to an impartial panel that gives reasons.
**Decision and penalty.** Findings and penalties are usually published, often with the registrant's name.
**Appeal** to the courts on the record.

blocks.text: Where the public is at serious risk, most regulators can suspend or restrict a registrant on an interim basis while the process runs.
Grounds for discipline

Unprofessional conduct or conduct unbecoming.

items.text: Practice reviews (or professional inspections) are **not** discipline. They check whether a registrant's practice, documents and processes meet standards, and lead to advice or, rarely, a referral to investigation.
They may be random, part of a program for a type of practice, or triggered by a concern.
Regulators also audit a sample of registrants' continuing professional development records each year.
Most regulators require firms that offer engineering or geoscience services to hold a **permit to practice** (or certificate of authorization).
The firm must name a responsible registrant who oversees professional practice, and keep a quality management system.

**BC note:** since 2 July 2021 every firm that practises professional engineering or geoscience in BC needs an EGBC permit to practice, including firms whose engineering is only for internal use, and municipalities and government bodies that practise. Firms must keep a professional practice management plan and can themselves be disciplined.
CPD keeps registrants competent as knowledge and technology change; most regulators make it mandatory.
In practice you plan your learning, do it, record it in your regulator's system, confirm compliance when you renew, and keep evidence in case your record is audited.
What counts varies by regulator, but courses, conferences and webinars, structured self-study, mentoring, technical committee work, and preparing papers or standards are commonly accepted.
Registrants who fail to comply can be suspended.

**BC note:** EGBC requires 60 hours of continuing education in each rolling three-year period, an annual learning plan based on a risk assessment of your practice, and annual reporting. Hours spent simply doing your job do not count.
The discipline standard of proof is the civil **balance of probabilities**, not beyond a reasonable doubt.
A practice review is not a disciplinary proceeding.
A complaint does not need to come from a client.
Criminal or civil proceedings do not prevent discipline for the same conduct.
Complaint → investigation → hearing → decision → appeal.
Penalties range from reprimand to cancellation, with costs and publication.
CPD: plan, do, record, declare, be audited.

lead.text: Real failures and court decisions turn the rules above into memorable stories; NPPE scenarios are often loosely based on them. Learn the lesson each one teaches rather than the details.

rows: The cantilever bridge collapsed during construction in 1907, killing 75 workers; the inquiry found the members were under-designed for the actual dead load and that warnings of deforming chords were not acted on. A second accident in 1916 killed 13 more
Check assumptions, supervise in person, act on warning signs. The Canadian Iron Ring ceremony, begun in 1925, reminds new engineers of this responsibility
Suspended walkways fell, killing 114. A change to the hanger-rod detail, approved through the shop-drawing process, doubled the load on a connection that was already weak
Review changes and shop drawings as carefully as the original design; the engineer who seals is responsible
Engineers warned that O-ring seals might fail in cold weather; managers overruled them and approved the launch. Seven crew died
When overruled on safety, put the risk in writing and escalate; public safety outranks schedule and employer pressure
A methane and coal-dust explosion killed 26 miners after repeated safety failures
Led to section 217.1 of the *Criminal Code*: those who direct work must take reasonable steps to prevent harm
E. coli contaminated the town's water; 7 people died and about 2,300 fell ill. Operators were poorly trained, and monitoring records were falsified
Competence, honest records and real oversight; led to Ontario's *Safe Drinking Water Act*
Algo Centre Mall, Elliot Lake, Ontario, 2012

A rooftop parking deck collapsed after years of water leakage corroded a steel connection, killing 2. The public inquiry criticized years of inspections that failed to identify or clearly report the danger
Inspection reports must be honest and complete; never let a client edit your conclusions. Report what you find, plainly, whoever pays for the report

The dam breached, releasing millions of cubic metres of water and tailings into nearby waterways. The independent review panel traced the failure to a weak glacial layer in the foundation that the design had not accounted for
Site investigation, independent review, environmental responsibility; the failure fed into BC's review of professional reliance and the *Professional Governance Act*

Employees can be personally liable in tort; may benefit from their employer's limitation clause
Engineers owe a duty of care to contractors who rely on their tender documents
Builders liable to later owners for repairing dangerous defects
Thin skull and crumbling skull rules
Privilege clause does not permit accepting a non-compliant bid
Employer's vicarious liability for employees' wrongs connected to the job
Test for a bona fide occupational requirement
Test for employee versus independent contractor
Damage must be a reasonably foreseeable type of harm
Breach of Contract A; test for enforcing exclusion clauses
Duty of honest performance in every contract
Expert witness's duty of impartiality to the court
Knowingly misleading the other party breaches honest performance

Contractual discretion must be exercised in good faith
