practice.title: NPPE practice questions
practice.author: Alireza Lotfollahzade
practice.note: Original practice questions written for study. They are not official NPPE questions.

questions.question: Why does a provincial legislature grant engineers the right to regulate themselves?

options.text: To limit competition from engineers trained abroad
To raise the income of qualified engineers
To reduce the cost of government
To protect the public by having qualified people set and enforce standards

questions.explanation: Self-regulation is a bargain: exclusive rights to title and practice are granted so the profession protects the public. Benefits to members are side effects, not the purpose.

questions.question: A new chemical engineering graduate has not yet applied to any regulator. Which title may she use on her business card?

options.text: Bachelor of Applied Science in Chemical Engineering

questions.explanation: Until she is registered with a regulator, she may not use 'engineer', 'EIT' or 'P.Eng.' in any form. Stating her degree is factual and allowed.

questions.question: Which activity most clearly falls within the reserved practice of professional engineering?

options.text: Selling engineering software to a client
Running a standard laboratory test by following a written procedure
Designing the relief system for a pressure vessel in a public facility
Drafting a drawing under instruction, with no design decisions

questions.explanation: Reserved practice needs both the application of engineering principles and something to safeguard (life, health, property, environment). Relief-system design has both.

questions.question: Why do engineering regulators' councils include public (lay) members?

options.text: To provide legal advice to council
To bring an outside, public-interest perspective to regulation

questions.explanation: Public members are not registrants. They add a public viewpoint and accountability to a self-regulating body.

questions.question: Which organization accredits undergraduate engineering programs in Canada?

options.text: The Canadian Society for Chemical Engineering
The Canadian Engineering Accreditation Board of Engineers Canada
The provincial regulator in each province

questions.explanation: Engineers Canada accredits programs through the CEAB. It does not license or discipline individuals; provincial regulators do.

questions.question: Which feature distinguishes a profession from other skilled occupations?

options.text: Its members belong to a union
It is self-regulated under statute and committed to serving the public

questions.explanation: Many occupations need degrees or pay well. A profession combines specialized knowledge with statutory self-regulation and a primary duty to the public.

questions.question: In Canadian engineering codes of ethics, which duty is paramount?

options.text: Duty to the safety, health and welfare of the public and the environment

questions.explanation: Every code puts public safety, health and welfare (now with the environment) first and makes all other duties subordinate when it is at stake.

questions.question: An engineer argues that a new highway is right because it benefits the largest number of people, even though a few residents lose their homes. Which theory is this?
questions.explanation: Weighing total benefits against harms to choose the greatest good for the greatest number is utilitarian (Mill). Rights ethics would focus on the displaced residents' rights.

questions.question: Which theory holds that the right action is a 'golden mean' between two extremes?
questions.explanation: Aristotle's virtue ethics describes virtues such as courage as a mean between excess and deficiency.

questions.question: A weakness most often attributed to duty (Kantian) ethics is that it:

options.text: Can justify harming a minority for the majority's benefit
Ignores the consequences of actions and offers no way to resolve conflicting duties

questions.explanation: Duty ethics judges acts by the rule followed, not outcomes, and gives little help when two duties clash. Harming a minority is the classic criticism of utilitarianism.

questions.question: An engineer owns shares in a pump manufacturer and is asked by a client to recommend pump suppliers. What should the engineer do first?

options.text: Sell the shares secretly and then recommend the manufacturer
Refuse to work for the client ever again
Recommend the manufacturer, since its pumps are good
Disclose the shareholding to the client in writing before advising

questions.explanation: Disclosure lets the client give informed consent or choose another adviser. If the interest could corrupt the advice, the engineer should step aside or divest.

questions.question: Which situation is a conflict of interest even if the engineer acts with complete honesty?

options.text: Reviewing, for a municipality, a design prepared by the engineer's own firm

questions.explanation: A perceived conflict damages trust even when judgment is sound. Reviewing your own firm's work for a regulator is a classic actual-or-perceived conflict.

questions.question: Management rejects an engineer's recommendation to use a more expensive coating. There is no safety or environmental risk either way. What should the engineer do?

options.text: Document the recommendation and its consequences, then accept the decision

questions.explanation: Where public safety is not at stake, the employer may make business decisions. The engineer's duty is to explain the consequences clearly, preferably in writing.

questions.question: A contractor whose change-order claims you assess offers you a weekend at a ski resort. You should:

options.text: Accept, and approve only half of the claims to show impartiality
Accept, because it does not affect your judgment

questions.explanation: Accepting a significant gift from a party whose claims you judge creates a conflict and the appearance of bias. Decline it.

questions.question: A client asks you to review drawings prepared by another engineer who is still engaged on the project. Ethically, you should:

options.text: Notify the other engineer that you have been asked to review the work
Offer to take over the project at a lower fee
Refuse, because reviewing another engineer's work is never allowed

questions.explanation: Codes require courtesy and fairness to colleagues: inform the engineer whose work you review (unless their engagement has ended). Undercutting to supplant them is unethical.

questions.question: During an assignment you learn from confidential client data that a structure open to the public is at risk of collapse. The client asks you to keep quiet. You should:

options.text: Urge the client to act, and if it will not, report to the appropriate authority
Keep the information confidential as the client asks

questions.explanation: Public safety overrides confidentiality. Give the client the chance to act first; if it refuses, report to the authority. Going to the media first, or staying silent, are both wrong.

questions.question: Under what conditions may an employed engineer do private consulting in the evenings?

options.text: Whenever the work is outside office hours
Never; moonlighting always breaches the code
When the employer knows, no employer resources or confidential information are used, and there is no competition with the employer
Only if the client is a relative

questions.explanation: Moonlighting is acceptable with disclosure and without using the employer's time, equipment, confidential information or competing with it.

questions.question: In a structured ethical decision process, what should come immediately after identifying the ethical problem?

options.text: Reporting the issue to the regulator
Seeking legal advice in every case

questions.explanation: Identify the issue, generate alternatives, evaluate them against law, code and theories, then decide and act. Scenarios often hide a third, better option.

questions.question: The standard of care expected of a professional engineer is that of:

options.text: A reasonably competent engineer in the same field and circumstances
An average member of the public
The leading expert in the country

questions.explanation: Courts judge professionals against a reasonably competent practitioner in the same discipline and circumstances at that time, not against perfection or the top expert.

questions.question: When may an engineer seal drawings that she did not personally prepare?

options.text: When they were prepared under her direct supervision, or she reviewed them thoroughly and accepts responsibility for them
When her manager instructs her to
When the drafting technician has more experience than she does

questions.explanation: A seal is acceptance of professional responsibility. It may go only on work prepared under the engineer's supervision or fully reviewed, and within her competence.

questions.question: Applying a professional seal to a report means that the engineer:

options.text: Guarantees the report is free of errors
Accepts professional responsibility for the work in it
Certifies the client's compliance with the law

questions.explanation: The seal shows who takes responsibility. It is not a warranty or a guarantee of perfection.

questions.question: Which document should normally not be sealed?

options.text: A draft report marked 'Preliminary, not for construction'
A final design drawing issued for construction
A final geotechnical report issued to a municipality

questions.explanation: Final documents issued for use by others are sealed. Drafts are marked preliminary instead, so nobody relies on them as final.

questions.question: A client buys insurance and signs a fixed-price contract to deal with cost-overrun risk. Which risk response is this?
questions.explanation: Insurance and fixed-price contracts shift the financial consequence to another party: risk transfer. Mitigation would reduce the likelihood or the impact itself.

questions.question: In a qualitative risk assessment, each risk is usually ranked on which two dimensions?

options.text: Probability of occurrence and severity of consequence

questions.explanation: A risk matrix ranks likelihood against consequence. Some methods add detectability (as in FMEA), but the core pair is probability and severity.

questions.question: Which control sits highest in the hierarchy of hazard controls?
questions.explanation: Elimination comes first, then substitution, engineering controls, administrative controls and finally PPE.

questions.question: Professional liability (errors and omissions) insurance for engineers is usually written on a claims-made basis. What does that mean?

options.text: It covers only claims made during the construction period
It pays only if the client makes the claim, not a third party
It covers claims first made while the policy is in force, so cover is needed after the engineer stops practising
It covers bodily injury caused by the engineer's car

questions.explanation: A claims-made policy responds to claims made during the policy period, regardless of when the work was done. Retiring engineers need run-off (tail) cover.

questions.question: Which policy is designed to cover a firm against third-party bodily injury and property damage from its operations, but not professional negligence?
questions.explanation: CGL covers bodily injury and property damage claims from operations and typically excludes professional services.

questions.question: A contractor goes bankrupt halfway through a project. Which instrument protects the owner's cost to complete the work?
questions.explanation: A surety's performance bond guarantees completion of the contract. A payment bond protects unpaid subcontractors and suppliers; a bid bond protects against a bidder refusing to sign.

questions.question: An engineer acting as a site supervisor is charged with an OH&S offence. Which defence is most likely to succeed?

options.text: The engineer did not intend the accident
Due diligence: proof that every reasonable precaution was taken
The regulation was not posted on site
The worker was a subcontractor's employee

questions.explanation: Most OH&S offences are strict liability. Lack of intent is no defence, but proving due diligence on a balance of probabilities is.

questions.question: What is the legal status of the National Building Code of Canada on its own?

options.text: It has no legal force until a province, territory or municipality adopts it
It is federal law that applies across Canada

questions.explanation: The NBC is a model code. It becomes law only when adopted, with or without amendments, by a jurisdiction such as a province.

questions.question: An engineer uses commercial finite-element software for a design. Who is responsible for the correctness of the results used in the design?

options.text: The engineer who uses and relies on the results
Nobody, if the software is widely used
The client who paid for the licence

questions.explanation: The professional must understand the software's limits, validate results with independent checks and remains accountable for the design.

questions.question: An engineer believes her company is releasing effluent above its permit limits. What should she normally do first?

options.text: Verify the facts and raise the issue internally, in writing
Post the evidence on social media

questions.explanation: Unless harm is imminent, check the facts and use internal routes first. Report to the regulator or authority if the company does not act.

questions.question: Sustainable development is best defined as development that:

options.text: Meets present needs without compromising future generations' ability to meet their own

questions.explanation: This is the Brundtland Commission definition (1987) used throughout Canadian engineering guidelines.

questions.question: Which standard sets requirements for an environmental management system?
questions.explanation: ISO 14001 is environmental management; ISO 9001 is quality management; ISO 45001 is occupational health and safety. CSA Z662 covers oil and gas pipeline systems.

questions.question: An engineer-in-training prepares calculations for a design. Who is professionally responsible for them?

options.text: The professional engineer who supervises, reviews and seals the work

questions.explanation: Trainees may practise only under the direct supervision of a registrant, who takes responsibility for the work by reviewing and sealing it.

questions.question: What is the standard of proof in a civil lawsuit for negligence?
questions.explanation: Civil claims are decided on a balance of probabilities (more likely than not). Beyond a reasonable doubt is the criminal standard.

questions.question: Which is an essential element of an enforceable contract?

options.text: A written document signed by both parties

questions.explanation: The elements are offer and acceptance, consideration, intention to create legal relations, capacity and legality. Most contracts need not be written.

questions.question: A contractor mails a bid to an owner on 1 March. The owner receives it on 4 March. When is the bid effective?

options.text: When the bid closing time passes
When the owner awards the contract
1 March, under the postal acceptance rule

questions.explanation: A bid is an offer, and offers are effective on receipt. The postal rule applies only to acceptances.

questions.question: Under the Contract A / Contract B framework, when does Contract A arise?

options.text: When the owner publishes the call for tenders
When a bidder submits a compliant bid
When the owner awards the construction contract

questions.explanation: Ron Engineering (1981): a compliant bid creates Contract A, typically making the bid irrevocable during its validity period. Contract B is the construction contract formed on award.

questions.question: Tender documents state that 'the lowest or any tender will not necessarily be accepted.' Can the owner accept the lowest bid even though it is non-compliant?

options.text: No, the privilege clause does not permit accepting a non-compliant bid
Only if the other bidders agree
Yes, the privilege clause allows any choice
Yes, if the bid is the cheapest

questions.explanation: M.J.B. Enterprises (1999): the owner owes compliant bidders an implied duty not to accept a non-compliant bid, despite a privilege clause.

questions.question: A clause in a contract drafted by the owner is ambiguous. A court will usually interpret it:

options.text: By asking an engineer to decide
Against the owner, who drafted it

questions.explanation: Contra proferentem: ambiguity is resolved against the party who drafted the clause.

questions.question: After signing a contract, a flood unforeseen by either party makes performance impossible. Which doctrine applies?
questions.explanation: Frustration ends a contract when an unforeseen event, not caused by either party, makes performance impossible or radically different. A force majeure clause may deal with the same event expressly.

questions.question: A supplier delivers a heat exchanger late. The owner's plant could not start, and the owner claims lost profits. Which principle limits the damages the owner can recover?

options.text: The owner can recover all losses, however remote
The losses must have been within the parties' reasonable contemplation when they contracted
Damages are always limited to the contract price

questions.explanation: Under Hadley v. Baxendale, recoverable losses are those arising naturally from the breach or within the parties' contemplation. The owner must also mitigate.

questions.question: A consultant performs extra work at the client's request but no price was ever agreed. On what basis can the consultant recover payment?
questions.explanation: Quantum meruit allows recovery of the reasonable value of work done where no enforceable price or contract exists.

questions.question: An engineer tries to assign her personal obligations under a professional services contract to a colleague without the client's consent. The result is most likely that:

options.text: The assignment of the obligations is not effective without the client's consent
The contract becomes void for both parties
The client must accept the colleague
The assignment is valid because all contracts are assignable

questions.explanation: Rights to payment can generally be assigned, but obligations to perform personal professional services cannot be transferred without the other party's consent.

questions.question: Which list states what a plaintiff must prove in a negligence action against an engineer?

options.text: Duty of care, breach of the standard of care, causation and damage
A signed contract and a breach

questions.explanation: Negligence requires a duty of care, a breach of the standard, causation (including foreseeable, not too remote, harm) and actual damage. No contract or intent is needed.

questions.question: An engineering firm prepares tender drawings for a highway owner. A contractor relies on them in its bid and loses money because they are wrong. Can the contractor sue the engineering firm even though they had no contract?

options.text: No, because engineers can only be sued by their clients
Yes, in negligence, because reliance by bidders was foreseeable
No, because of privity of contract

questions.explanation: Edgeworth Construction v. N.D. Lea (1993): the firm owed a duty of care to contractors who foreseeably relied on its tender documents. Privity limits contract claims, not tort claims.

questions.question: Two contractors' separate negligence caused one flood. Under joint and several liability, the plaintiff:

options.text: Can recover only half from each
Must sue both together or recover nothing
Can recover the full damages from either contractor

questions.explanation: Each joint tortfeasor can be made to pay the whole loss; they then sort out contribution between themselves.

questions.question: An employee of an engineering firm makes a negligent error while doing her assigned work. Who can be held liable?

options.text: Neither, because it was an honest mistake
The firm vicariously, and the employee personally

questions.explanation: Employers are vicariously liable for employees' torts in the course of employment, and the employee remains personally liable for her own negligence.

questions.question: A Canadian firm has a valuable, unpatented manufacturing process that competitors cannot see. Which protection best suits it?

options.text: Trade secret protection, backed by confidentiality measures

questions.explanation: A secret process can be protected indefinitely as a trade secret if the firm takes reasonable steps to keep it confidential. Copyright protects expression, not processes.

questions.question: Which is the term of a Canadian patent?

options.text: Life of the inventor plus 70 years
20 years from the filing date, subject to maintenance fees

questions.explanation: Canadian patents last up to 20 years from filing, if annual maintenance fees are paid.

questions.question: An inventor presents her new catalyst at a conference before filing a patent application. What is the effect in Canada?

options.text: She can never obtain a patent anywhere
The disclosure has no effect on patentability
She has 12 months from her disclosure to file in Canada, but may lose rights in countries without a grace period

questions.explanation: Canada (like the US) gives a 12-month grace period for the applicant's own disclosure. Many countries, including in Europe, give none.

questions.question: A consulting engineer, working as an independent contractor without a written agreement, prepares calculation software for a client. Who owns the copyright?

options.text: It is in the public domain

questions.explanation: Absent an agreement, the author owns copyright. The employer-ownership rule applies to employees, not independent contractors.

questions.question: An engineer retained as an expert witness by the plaintiff owes her primary duty to:
questions.explanation: An expert's overriding duty is to assist the court impartially (White Burgess, 2015). A contingency fee would compromise that independence.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of the holdback required by construction lien legislation?

options.text: To pay the owner's legal costs
To create a fund from which valid lien claims of subcontractors and suppliers can be paid

questions.explanation: Holdbacks (typically 10 %) limit the owner's lien exposure and ensure money is available for those down the payment chain.

questions.question: Which statement about workers' compensation in Canada is correct?

options.text: Workers must prove the employer was at fault to receive benefits
It applies only to unionized workers
It is no-fault insurance, and in exchange workers generally cannot sue their employer
It is a federal program administered by the Canada Revenue Agency

questions.explanation: Provincial workers' compensation pays benefits regardless of fault and bars most lawsuits against employers.

questions.question: Which is one of the three basic rights of workers under Canadian OH&S legislation?

options.text: The right to refuse unsafe work without reprisal
The right to a pay increase after an accident
The right to choose their supervisor
The right to inspect the employer's financial records

questions.explanation: Workers have the right to know about hazards, to participate in health and safety, and to refuse unsafe work.

questions.question: An employer requires all field engineers to pass a demanding fitness test. When is this requirement lawful despite its discriminatory effect?

options.text: When it is a bona fide occupational requirement and accommodation is impossible without undue hardship
Whenever the employer believes it is useful

questions.explanation: Under the Meiorin test, a standard must be rationally connected to the job, adopted in good faith and reasonably necessary, with accommodation to the point of undue hardship.

questions.question: What can a mediator do that an arbitrator normally does not?

options.text: Meet privately with each party to explore settlement

questions.explanation: Mediators facilitate a voluntary settlement and often caucus with each side. Arbitrators hear evidence and make a binding award.

questions.question: Which statement about law in Quebec is correct?

options.text: Quebec uses English common law for contracts
Quebec's criminal law differs from the rest of Canada
Patent law does not apply in Quebec
Quebec's private law is based on the Civil Code of Quebec, while federal laws such as the Criminal Code apply as elsewhere

questions.explanation: Quebec's private law (contracts, property, liability) is codified in the Civil Code; federal law, including criminal and patent law, is the same across Canada.

questions.question: Which instrument ranks highest in the legal framework of an engineering regulator?

options.text: The Act passed by the legislature

questions.explanation: The Act is the statute. Regulations and bylaws are made under it and cannot conflict with it.

questions.question: A person who is not registered keeps practising engineering after warnings from the regulator. Which remedy can stop the ongoing practice?

options.text: An injunction from a superior court

questions.explanation: Discipline applies only to registrants. Against non-registrants the regulator uses enforcement: prosecution for an offence and an injunction to restrain continued practice.

questions.question: Which is most likely to be misuse of a protected title?

options.text: An EIT registered with the regulator using 'EIT'
A graduate describing her B.Eng. degree on a CV
An unregistered person advertising services as 'Professional Engineer'

questions.explanation: Using 'Professional Engineer' or 'P.Eng.' without registration is holding out, an offence even if no engineering is performed.

questions.question: Which requirement is common to all Canadian engineering regulators for professional registration?
questions.explanation: All regulators assess good character, along with academic qualifications, experience, professional practice knowledge and language. Citizenship and society membership are not required.

questions.question: How does a technical society differ from a regulator?

options.text: A technical society disciplines members for breaches of the code
A technical society licenses engineers in specialized fields
A technical society advances technical knowledge; it does not regulate practice

questions.explanation: Regulators are statutory bodies that license and discipline to protect the public. Societies are voluntary bodies that share technical knowledge.

questions.question: What standard of proof applies in a professional discipline hearing in Canada?
questions.explanation: Discipline is a civil-type proceeding: the regulator must prove its case on a balance of probabilities, with clear and cogent evidence.

questions.question: Which conduct is most likely to lead to disciplinary action?

options.text: Declining an assignment outside one's competence
Charging a fee higher than a competitor's
Sealing drawings for a type of project outside one's demonstrated competence

questions.explanation: Practising and sealing outside one's competence breaches every code of ethics and is a common ground for discipline.

questions.question: Who can file a complaint about a registrant with the regulator?

options.text: Anyone, including members of the public, colleagues and the regulator itself

questions.explanation: Complaints can come from anyone with a concern; the regulator can also start its own investigation.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a practice review of an individual registrant?

options.text: To assess and improve the registrant's practice against standards

questions.explanation: Practice reviews are educational and preventive. Serious concerns found in a review may be referred to investigation, but the review itself is not discipline.

questions.question: Which is not a typical penalty available to a discipline panel?

options.text: Payment of investigation and hearing costs
An order to take a course or exam

questions.explanation: Discipline panels can reprimand, fine, restrict, suspend or cancel, order education and costs, and publish. Only a criminal court can imprison.

questions.question: Why is continuing professional development considered a core element of professionalism?

options.text: It keeps practitioners competent as knowledge and technology change
It generates revenue for the regulator
It is required only for engineers in management
It replaces the need for supervision

questions.explanation: Competence is not fixed at licensing; CPD programs require registrants to keep their knowledge current, report it and be audited.
